claim: Outside wet-bulb temperature at the 35 °C, 30 % RH design point is 21.5 °C
law: Psychrometrics; independent check with the Stull (2011) wet-bulb fit

claim: Air leaving the pad (23.1 °C) stays above the wet-bulb temperature, the limit of direct evaporative cooling
law: Adiabatic saturation: direct evaporative cooling cannot go below the wet bulb

claim: A 150 mm cellulose pad reaches about 88 % saturation effectiveness at 0.52 m/s face velocity
law: NTU model calibrated to 75 % at 0.6 m/s for 100 mm (CAL assumption); maker data for deeper pads show 90 % or more (CELdek)
check: Within the range makers publish; the chosen pad's own chart is not yet in hand (ZBX-DEC-001 to confirm 2). The drop is set by it: PR-002 (8 K) holds down to about 68 % effectiveness (independent review)

claim: Two 400 m³/h fans deliver about 563 m³/h through the pad, shutters and guards
law: A bound only: fan delivery cannot exceed the free-air flow of the two fans in parallel (800 m³/h); the operating point itself rests on S5

claim: The fan curve and the wet pad's pressure drop give the 18 Pa operating point
law: Straight-line fan curve to a 50 to 70 Pa shut-off; wet 100 mm pad 15 Pa at 1.0 m/s (CAL assumptions)
check: Assumed curves; supplier data for the chosen fan and pad needed (ZBX-DEC-001 to confirm 2). At only about 18 Pa, a 3 m/s wind on the pad wall (about 5 Pa) moves the flow by 15 to 20 %, and in hold mode (one fan at 30 %, about 5 Pa shut-off) it can stall or reverse the flow (independent review)

claim: Store air warms about 2.35 K from supply to exhaust while it absorbs the 443 W heat load
law: Steady-flow energy balance, rise = Q / (rho V cp), rho 1.15 kg/m3

claim: Mean store air is 10.7 K below outside air at the design point
law: The store cannot be cooler than the supply air, so the drop is below effectiveness x wet-bulb depression (tighter bound, independent review)

claim: The pad evaporates about 32 L of water on the design day (10 h of cooling)
law: Latent heat taken up equals the sensible heat given up by the air, h_fg 2.43 MJ/kg

claim: Mean store RH is about 81 % while cooling at the design point
law: Moisture balance with the Magnus saturation pressure
closed_by: ZBX-CAL-001 s5; rests on S3 (about 1 point of RH per point of effectiveness)

claim: One 150 W panel covers the 372 Wh design day (10 h cooling, 2 h evening ventilation)
law: Energy balance; at 40 % losses (PWM, dust, harmattan haze, cable) the panel gives 450 Wh, still 21 % over (independent review)

claim: A 150 W panel of 1,480 x 670 mm
law: Module efficiency at 1,000 W/m2 below the Shockley-Queisser limit for one junction

claim: The 12.8 V, 12 Ah battery carries the 62 Wh used after sunset
law: Energy balance

claim: A 20 A PWM charge controller suits the 150 W panel
law: Controller rating at least 1.25 x the panel's short-circuit current (9 A); it must also have a LiFePO4 charge profile (about 14.2 to 14.4 V), no lead-acid temperature compensation and a low-voltage disconnect (BOM line 11)

claim: Two 12 W fans move 563 m³/h at about 18 Pa
law: Air power Q x dp cannot exceed the 24 W of electrical input (implied fan efficiency about 12 %, usual for small axial fans)

claim: A 6 W pump lifts 3.6 L/min to the header 2 m up
law: Hydraulic power rho g H Q cannot exceed the electrical input

claim: The 1.5 mm² load cable in the 45 °C roof space is protected by its fuse
law: Fuse rating I_n <= derated cable capacity I_z (IEC 60364-5-52 tables B.52.4 and B.52.14, to confirm against the edition used); 5 A load fuse at the source end of the run after the fix; both fuses DC rated with a breaking capacity above the battery's short-circuit current (D5)
closed_by: ZBX-DEC-001 D1 (fix under the standing instruction); ZBX-CAL-001 s9

claim: Each roof post footing holds down its share of the uplift at a 30 m/s gust
law: Footing weight against net uplift per post, with a factor of at least 1.5, at a 30 m/s gust and a mean net Cp of 1.5; the factor falls below 1.5 above about 32 m/s, and edge zones of a canopy reach Cp about 2 (independent review; ZBX-DEC-001 D7)

claim: The 50 x 150 mm purlins carry the uplift on a 0.7 m strip over 3.7 m
law: Simply supported beam, sigma = M / Z; sawn softwood about 7 MPa allowed (grade to confirm); at an edge-zone Cp of 2.0 the stress reaches about 6.9 MPa (D7)

claim: The 75 x 150 mm roof beams span 2.8 m between posts
law: Simply supported beam under the uplift less the sheet weight

claim: Each purlin end needs a tie of 2 kN rated uplift
law: Tie load from the purlin's uplift, half at each end; edge purlins carry more and the nails must hold the rating in the timber (D7)

claim: Shelf rails carry four 22 kg crates over 1.05 m
law: Simply supported 50 x 75 mm rail, sigma = M / Z

claim: The 7 t of brick bears on a 450 mm strip footing
law: Bearing pressure against about 100 kPa allowed on firm soil; not valid on expansive clay or collapsible sand, so the site soil is to check

claim: Dry loose rice husk conducts about 0.06 W/(m·K)
law: Measured 0.065 to 0.075 W/(m·K) for rice husk insulators (Cigarruista Solis et al. 2024)
closed_by: ZBX-CAL-001 s4.1 (at 0.075 the wall gain rises by about 14 W, about 0.1 K in the store; the review recommends 0.07 central and 0.06 to 0.09 in the scenarios at the next CAL revision)

claim: Mixed produce near 25 °C gives off about 0.15 W/kg of respiration heat
law: Respiration classes at 5 °C (Kader 2002), about 5 x at 25 °C; 10.7 J per mg CO2 from glucose oxidation
closed_by: ZBX-CAL-001 s4 (at 0.22 W/kg the store is about 0.2 K warmer, inside the unfavorable case at 0.25 W/kg)

claim: Tomato shelf life rises at least 1.5 times over ambient storage in the dry season
law: Zero energy cool chambers raised tomato shelf life from 6 to 11 days (e-planet 18(2)); D-Lab Mali reported 10 days against 2 to 4 for peppers and eggplant
check: Evidence comes from cooler, more humid passive chambers; a paired storage trial with the partner is needed (TRL 4)

claim: Produce loses 0.5 to 2 % of its mass a day as water vapor, adding about 0.3 g/kg to the airstream
law: Transpiration allowance bracketing leafy and fruit crops; it moves store RH by under 2 percentage points
check: Bracketed by the favorable and unfavorable cases

claim: A covered, shaded sump drained weekly, a daily bleed and a pad dried out at the end of every cooling day keep Legionella growth low
law: WHO, Legionella and the prevention of legionellosis (2007): stagnant warm water (25 to 45 °C), sediment and biofilm favour growth; drain, clean and keep systems dry. Exposure route: the pad's drift is carried through the room past people entering
check: Controls follow the guidance: daily dry-out (pump off 60 min before the fans stop) and the bleed added (D5); fans run 10 min before entry; disinfection of the sump proposed (D8); sump water never touches produce

claim: With at least one air change an hour the store's CO2 stays below a 5,000 ppm workplace limit
law: Steady-state CO2 rise = produce CO2 / ventilation; 480 kg at about 50 mg CO2/(kg h)

claim: Fired brick in the pad wall stays strong when wet
law: Fired clay is a ceramic and does not soften in water, unlike unfired earth

claim: Aluminium panel frames with stainless bolts on a galvanised roof do not corrode in a dry inland climate
law: Zinc and aluminium sit close in the galvanic series; small stainless fasteners in a large aluminium area corrode little in dry, unpolluted air
check: Aluminium is anodic to stainless, so EPDM isolating washers go under every stainless bolt on the aluminium frames by default (D5); inspection each season

claim: A lithium iron phosphate battery with a BMS, kept shaded and charged between 0 and 45 °C, is safe in this duty
law: LiFePO4 has a higher thermal-runaway onset than cobalt-based cells; makers limit charging to about 0 to 45 °C. In a shaded box on the outside wall at 35 to 40 °C air, charging at 0.69 C self-heats the pack toward that limit, so the BMS may stop charging at midday (independent review)
check: Safe, because the BMS stops charging; the energy lost on the hottest days is to assess. Moving the power box into the cooled store is proposed to Amish (ZBX-DEC-001 D6)

claim: Low-cost sensors resolve the 4 K wet-bulb depression threshold
law: Depression error from +-3 % RH and +-0.5 K at 30 °C, 75 % RH, against a quarter of the threshold; sun on an unshielded sensor would add 2 to 3 K, so the six-plate shield and a field calibration at TRL 4 are part of the claim

claim: 563 m³/h is 331 cfm and about 78 air changes an hour in the 7.2 m³ room

The favorable to unfavorable range of the drop (9.8 to 11.4 K) brackets the inputs varied in the three scenarios (pad effectiveness, wall wetting, respiration, fan shut-off, leaks, sun, roof space, ground, transpiration); husk conductivity, the pad pressure-drop law, wind on the pad and sensor error are not varied (independent review)
law: Three-scenario bracketing of every uncertain input (CAL Table 1)

claim: The shaded roof space stays near 40 °C (38 to 43 °C) on the design day
law: Allowance for a ventilated 450 mm gap under a sunlit sheet roof; ceiling gain 46 W in the central case
check: Assumption; a roof-space temperature log is needed (TRL 4)

claim: The battery covers the controller and hold-mode ventilation through cloudy spells
law: 123 Wh usable; hold mode about 2 W plus the 1 W controller lasts about 40 h with no sun; beyond that the fans stop and the room is sealed
check: A passive vent for the no-power case is proposed to Amish (ZBX-DEC-001 D3)

claim: The daily bleed keeps the pad water at no more than 4 cycles of concentration, so hard water does not scale the pad
law: Cycles of concentration = (evaporation + bleed) / bleed; cellulose pads scale above about 3 to 5 cycles in typical water (independent review). The TRL 3 design's 4 L bleed gave about 9 cycles; fixed (D5)
closed_by: ZBX-DEC-001 D5; ZBX-CAL-001 s8 (bleed 10.6 L, total 43 L/day)

claim: Option B holds the full room about 3 K below outside air at the design point
law: Wall-to-wet-cavity balance with stack ventilation; ZECCs measured 4.4 to 5.0 K monthly mean, 7.25 K best day (e-planet 18(2))

claim: Option B uses about 70 L of water a day
law: Evaporation from the wet outer leaf (Lewis relation) plus the cavity's conduction loss

claim: A low vent and a roof stack of 0.02 m² each give option B at least one air change an hour
law: Stack flow Q = Cd A sqrt(2 g h dT / T), Cd 0.6, 1.6 m between openings; the room is cooler than outside, so cool air drains out of the low vent and 35 °C air enters at the stack (direction noted by the independent review)

claim: Option B keeps the room humid (55 to 90 % RH)
law: A moisture balance with produce transpiration alone and the B3 flow gives about 55 % RH (independent review); ZECCs report high humidity because their inner faces are wet
check: Depends on how wet the inner leaf runs; to assess

claim: A damp, slowly ventilated chamber grows mold on walls and produce unless cleaned and aired
law: High humidity and little air movement favour mold; D-Lab notes cleaning and airing practice

claim: Option C holds the room about 7 K below outside air at the design point, in a light wind
law: Wet-wall effectiveness 0.75 (Wayua et al. 2012 measured 74 to 87 % and 10.5 K at 14:00) and a heat balance on the ventilator flow
check: First-order 6.9 K at 250 m³/h; conditional on C2, so it cannot be closed while C2 is open (independent review)

claim: A 300 mm turbine ventilator draws about 250 m³/h in a light wind
law: Wind-driven extraction; no rated airflow found in the maker listing checked (MKT); calm days give little flow
check: To assess with the maker's chart; option C's cooling scales with it

claim: Option C uses about 40 L of water a day
law: Latent heat balance on the ventilator flow plus drip losses of about 20 L

claim: Galvanised mesh lasts in permanently wet charcoal
law: Wet carbon is an electrical conductor and noble to zinc; contact can speed corrosion of the galvanising
check: Mesh life to assess; stainless or plastic mesh is the fallback

claim: Wet charcoal walls stay free of mold and smell
law: Permanently wet organic-carbon media can grow mold; charcoal coolers are washed and the charcoal replaced
